subtype: Approach: identify the underlying value behind the anger [Thinking]
passage:
Dinner at my grandparents' flat got loud fast. Saurabh mama slapped the table and said the election result would wreck everything, and my cousin shouted back. Normally I'd have joined one side. That night I kept quiet and thought: he isn't angry about a party, he's angry about something. Slogans are just where it comes out.

So when there was a gap, I asked, "Mama, what are you actually afraid of?" He was quiet, then said, "That the shop will go under, and that you kids won't be safe. I've seen bad years." I realised I wanted the same things: safe family, steady work. We disagreed on how, but under the shouting there was something we shared. Suraj

qa.q: What did Saurabh mama say he was afraid of?
qa.a: That the shop will go under and that the kids won't be safe.

qa.q: What was Saurabh mama really feeling under the shouting, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Saurabh mama was afraid for the shop and the family's safety, which the quiet pause and the words "I've seen bad years" reveal.

qa.q: What could Suraj try next in a conversation with Saurabh mama, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could ask which of those worries feels most pressing and what he has seen in the bad years, because listening to the concern builds trust for a later talk about solutions.

qa.q: How might the cousin who shouted back feel when Suraj asks this question?
qa.a: The cousin may feel surprised that the argument paused, and may see that the shouting had been about worry rather than winning.

grounding: In a heated dinner debate, the student asks what the uncle actually fears and sees that a shared value lies beneath the position.
